1	# Task 10: Fireworks display over a night harbor
2	
3	Build a single-page browser app with the provided framework, served by vite, rendering to the canvas with id #app. The scene is a fireworks display at night over a calm harbor. Show a dark star-dusted night sky, a water surface that faintly reflects the light of the bursts, and a low dark silhouette of a shoreline or pier with a few small buildings or boats. Rockets launch from the shoreline one after another at irregular intervals, rise with a short glowing trail, and burst into spherical shells of many glowing sparks. Use at least three clearly different burst colors (for example gold, red, and blue or green), and make each burst fade and fall under gravity over a second or two before it disappears. Some bursts should leave trailing streaks. The sky and water should be lit subtly by the active bursts. The scene must animate continuously without user input, with a slow gentle camera drift or a fixed camera framing the sky and harbor. Aim for a polished, cinematic look: strong glow on the sparks against a dark background, no flat or washed-out colors, no visible geometry artifacts. Keep it smooth at interactive frame rates. Also expose window.__TASK_STATE__ = { bursts: <total number of bursts that have exploded so far>, activeParticles: <current number of live spark particles> } and update it every frame.

content.thinking:
I can declare custom attributes like aVel in the vertex shader using camelCase naming to pass validation. I'm designing a single static geometry acting as a ring buffer of particle slots, where each spark is a quad of 4 vertices carrying per-vertex attributes like origin position and birth time.

Rather than re-uploading geometry every burst, I'm thinking I could precompute the entire animation deterministically as a fixed pool of bursts with absolute launch times, then use time modulo a period in the shader to loop it infinitely while still appearing irregularly spaced.

Even better: make each burst its own mesh node from a shared pool (say 8 slots), each with a static sphere-direction geometry, and drive the variation purely through uniforms set at launch time—origin, color, start time, speed, type. That keeps runtime updates limited to uniform changes rather than geometry rewrites, and I can apply the same pooled-uniform approach to rocket trails, treating each trail spark as a node with its own launch position, apex, and timing uniforms.

Trail length varies by burst type, long for streak bursts, short for dot-like ones. To get curved trails rather than straight approximations, I'll build each spark as a short ribbon of segments (4-5) sampled at earlier times, fading alpha along its length — roughly 3600 verts per burst, ~29k total across 8 slots, still cheap.

For sphere-shaped bursts I'll generate directions with a jittered fibonacci sphere distribution and pack per-spark randomness into one attribute shared across a spark's vertices, while burst-level uniforms (origin, start time, colors, speed, trail length, life, seed) control variation between the different burst instances.

For counting live particles, I realize I need JS to mirror the shader's per-spark lifetime logic: since each spark's life depends on its random factor, I'll precompute a lifeFactor array in JS so I can count sparks whose age is still under their lifetime each frame, including both burst sparks and rocket trail heads.

This is getting too complicated — I'll simplify by treating the rocket as a ribbon-style trail instead of individual particles, with points tracking backward in time over a fixed trail length.

I decide to count only burst sparks as live particles, skipping rockets-in-flight from the count to keep the physics model clean, and I'm working out the gravity-affected position formula using velocity with drag decay plus a quadratic gravity term.

Now I'm blocking out the scene geometry: camera positioned low over the water looking toward a distant shoreline at z=-60 where a silhouette of pier, buildings, and boats sits, with rocket launches originating from the shore and bursts happening at height 25-40 with roughly 12-unit radius.

I'm working through the camera math to get burst sizing right relative to screen width—checking field-of-view angles against distance to the shore to make sure the fireworks read as appropriately scaled against a 640x360 frame, adjusting shore distance and camera position until the proportions feel correct.

Lowering the target to y=12 gives too much water at only 42%, so I'm adjusting the burst centers to y 18-30 with radius 10-13 to keep them from clipping the sky, though there's still slight overflow near the top I need to watch.

I should add water reflections too - mirroring burst sparks below the water plane with dimmer alpha and ripple distortion. The tricky part is depth testing: since the water surface is opaque, I need it rendered first and have the reflected sparks drawn additively without failing depth, so the reflection shows through properly.

Maybe simpler: give the water mesh a transparent, depth-write-off material so it sits in the transparent pass, and draw reflection sparks with depthTest off and additive blending so they layer naturally over the water without fighting the opaque shore silhouette.

If sparks draw as transparent additive after opaque geometry, with water skipping depth writes but shore writing depth, the shore buildings at the same z-range as their mirrored reflections would naturally occlude portions of those reflections correctly, while real sparks behind the shore stay properly hidden too.

I should double check whether blending is specified as "additive" with transparent and depthWrite set appropriately, and whether bloom is applied as a post-processing effect.

For the background, I want a gradient sky with stars rather than a flat void, so I'm considering using a sky.gradient helper with a stars option. Since the sky can't be lit by scene lights directly, I'm thinking about building a custom sky dome shader that takes burst positions and colors as uniforms to render glows directly into the gradient, combined with hash-based star generation.

I'm going with a large inverted sphere behind the camera with a custom fragment shader driven by world direction, since I have no way to preview output and need to stay conservative with well-documented shader behavior to avoid tone-mapping or color-space surprises.

I'll skip the "looks.preset" shortcut and hand-build the scene with background and bloom effects instead, so I should check how other night recipes configure bloom and uniforms before finalizing the shader setup.

I need to watch out for shared material specs causing uniforms to leak across nodes—each slot needs its own material.custom instance. I'm also reconsidering timing: rather than relying on a shared time uniform, I'll set my own per-node time uniform each frame, which is cheap even across many nodes.

Now I need to check how setUniform handles vector types and whether the uniform value validation supports vec3/vec4 arrays, so I'm going to look at the runtimeNodes setUniform and validation logic.

I need each node to have a unique runtime ID for keyed writes, and I'm thinking about only updating the clock uniform per node per frame to limit overhead, skipping redundant uniform updates when values haven't changed. I could also avoid per-frame clock updates entirely by relying on an engine-level time uniform instead of pushing time from the JS side.

For the burst effects, I'm trying to figure out how to pack position, intensity, and color data for six burst slots affecting sky and water without exceeding reasonable per-frame uniform counts, since vec4 arrays aren't well supported and I need separate uniforms per slot for direction/intensity and color -- which adds up to a lot of calls. I'm considering packing color as a palette index instead of a full vec3 to cut down the uniform count.

Counting it up: 6 burst + 4 rocket + 6 mirror burst + 4 mirror rockets + sky + water comes to 22 setUniform calls per frame, which feels heavy compared to a reference recipe doing just one. To cut this down, I'm considering merging mirror and real geometry into a single mesh with a per-vertex flag that flips y in the vertex shader, letting mirrored sparks share material and draw calls with the real ones.

Since water doesn't write depth, mirrored sparks rendering below it is fine, so one node per burst slot with doubled vertices should work, and the same trick applies to rockets. That gets me down to 6 burst nodes + 3 rocket nodes + sky + water, about 11 clocks per frame, which seems manageable -- I briefly wonder if I can avoid separate clocks by reading elapsed time directly from the frame callback, but I'll just stick with JS clocks via performance.now for simplicity. Now I need to make sure window.__TASK_STATE__ updates every frame and __EVAL_READY__ fires after the first frame renders, once app.ready() resolves.

For performance under software WebGL2 rendering, I'm keeping spark counts modest since this will likely run on SwiftShader in headless Chromium, so vertex counts stay in the thousands, well within budget. For timing determinism I'll use a real clock with per-frame dt clamping (max 0.1s) accumulated into a simulation clock, so burst scheduling stays consistent even if headless rendering throttles frame rate. I'm planning the first rocket launch around t=0.3s with burst at t=1.5s, then irregular bursts every 0.8-2.2s, allowing for up to 3-4 simultaneous bursts within the 6 available slots given each burst's ~2.6s lifetime.
